topic: Public Administration — Meaning, Nature, Scope & Evolution

items.title: Meaning, Nature & Scope of Public Administration
items.body:
### What public administration is, and how wide it reaches

**In one line**
Public administration is the machinery and process by which government puts law and public policy into action to serve the people.

**Why it is asked**
The integral-versus-managerial debate, POSDCORB, and the public-versus-private distinction are foundational and recur as direct MCQs and essay openings.

**The story**
**Public administration** is the management of public affairs — the machinery and the processes through which government **implements law and public policy**. Two classic definitions capture it: **L.D. White** called it 'all operations having for their purpose the fulfilment or enforcement of public policy', and **Woodrow Wilson** called it 'government in action... the most visible side of government'.
Scholars dispute how wide it reaches. The **integral view** (Henri Fayol, L.D. White) counts *all* activities — managerial, clerical, technical, manual — needed to achieve public purposes. The **managerial view** (Luther Gulick, W.F. Willoughby) counts only the top-level management functions, captured by the acronym **POSDCORB**. Its **scope** can be mapped by process (POSDCORB) or by subject-matter (defence, revenue, health, welfare). As a field it is both an art (getting things done) and a developing social science.

**Picture it — the two views of nature**

| View | Champions | What it covers |
|---|---|---|
| Integral view | Henri Fayol, L.D. White | ALL activities (managerial, clerical, technical, manual) |
| Managerial view | Gulick, Willoughby | ONLY the top managers' functions (POSDCORB) |

**Terms explained**
- **POSDCORB** — Planning, Organising, Staffing, Directing, Co-ordinating, Reporting, Budgeting: the seven management functions.
- **Integral view** — administration = every activity needed to fulfil public purposes.
- **Managerial view** — administration = only the managerial work of senior officials.
- **Subject-matter view** — mapping administration by the fields it covers (defence, health, revenue).

**Public vs private administration**
Public administration works under **political direction, the rule of law, public accountability, a non-profit purpose and public scrutiny**, unlike private management, which is driven mainly by profit.

**Don't confuse**
- **Integral vs managerial view** — integral = all activities; managerial = only POSDCORB-type functions.
- **Public vs private administration** — public is bound by law, accountability and non-profit service; private is profit-led.

**Remember it**
POSDCORB order = 'Please Own Some Data Cause Reports Balance'.

**TL;DR**
- Public administration = machinery/process by which government implements law and policy.
- Integral view (Fayol, White) = all activities; managerial view (Gulick, Willoughby) = POSDCORB functions only.
- Scope mapped by process (POSDCORB) and by subject-matter (defence, revenue, welfare).
- It differs from private administration by political direction, rule of law, accountability and non-profit purpose.
keyPoints: Public Administration = the machinery/process by which government implements law and public policy.
Integral view (Fayol, L.D. White) = all activities; Managerial view (Gulick, Willoughby) = only POSDCORB-type management functions.
POSDCORB = Planning, Organising, Staffing, Directing, Co-ordinating, Reporting, Budgeting.
Scope mapped two ways: by process (POSDCORB) and by subject-matter (defence, revenue, welfare...).
Public administration differs from private by political direction, rule of law, public accountability and non-profit purpose.
items.mnemonic: POSDCORB order: 'Please Own Some Data Cause Reports Balance'.
items.source: Standard texts on Public Administration (Wilson 1887; L.D. White; Gulick & Urwick 1937)

items.title: Evolution of Public Administration as a Discipline
items.body:
### How the discipline evolved, from Wilson to good governance

**In one line**
Public administration grew from Woodrow Wilson's 1887 call to study it separately, through the 'principles' and bureaucracy era, to behavioural critiques and today's good-governance paradigm.

**Why it is asked**
The sequence of paradigms, their flag-bearers and signature phrases ('steering not rowing', 'serving not steering') are classic matching-type MCQs and essay scaffolding.

**The story**
The discipline begins in **1887**, when **Woodrow Wilson's** essay 'The Study of Administration' first argued that administration should be studied as a **distinct discipline** — making him the father of public administration. Wilson and **Frank Goodnow (1900)** proposed the **politics-administration dichotomy**: politics expresses the state's will (policy), administration executes it. This was later criticised as unrealistic because administrators also shape policy. The early 20th century stressed **efficiency** (F.W. Taylor's scientific management) and **principles**, peaking with **POSDCORB (Gulick and Urwick, 1937)**; alongside, **Max Weber** described the **rational-legal** 'ideal-type' bureaucracy — hierarchy, rules, files, impersonality and merit careers.
Then came a **behavioural turn** — Elton Mayo's human relations, Herbert Simon's attack on the 'proverbs of administration' — and a succession of paradigms, each reacting to the last.

**Picture it — the paradigms**

| Paradigm | Marker | Core idea |
|---|---|---|
| New Public Administration | Minnowbrook I, 1968 (Waldo); Marini 1971 | Social equity, relevance, values |
| New Public Management | Hood 1991; Osborne and Gaebler 1992 | Market managerialism, 'steering not rowing' |
| New Public Service | Denhardt and Denhardt (2000/2003) | 'Serving not steering', democratic citizenship |
| Good Governance | UNESCAP eight attributes | Participation, transparency, accountability |

**Terms explained**
- **Politics-administration dichotomy** — the idea that policy-making (politics) and policy-execution (administration) are separate.
- **Rational-legal bureaucracy** — Weber's ideal-type: authority based on rules and offices, not persons.
- **New Public Management (NPM)** — reforms importing market and managerial methods into government.
- **'Steering not rowing'** — Osborne and Gaebler's slogan: government should set direction, not deliver everything itself.
- **Good governance** — the current paradigm: participation, rule of law, transparency, accountability, responsiveness, equity, effectiveness.

**Don't confuse**
- **NPM vs New Public Service** — NPM treats the citizen as a customer and 'steers'; New Public Service treats the citizen as a citizen and 'serves'.
- **Wilson vs Goodnow** — Wilson founded the study (1887); Goodnow refined the dichotomy (1900).

**Remember it**
'Wilson (1887) → dichotomy → POSDCORB/Weber → NPA (equity) → NPM (steer) → NPS (serve) → good governance.'

**TL;DR**
- Woodrow Wilson (1887) founded the discipline; Goodnow (1900) refined the politics-administration dichotomy.
- POSDCORB (Gulick and Urwick, 1937) marked the 'principles' era; Weber gave the rational-legal bureaucracy.
- New Public Administration (Minnowbrook, 1968) added social equity.
- NPM (Hood 1991; Osborne-Gaebler 1992) = 'steering not rowing'; New Public Service (Denhardt) = 'serving not steering'; good governance is the current paradigm.
keyPoints: Woodrow Wilson (1887) founded the discipline; politics-administration dichotomy refined by Frank Goodnow (1900).
POSDCORB (Gulick & Urwick, 1937) marked the 'principles of administration' era.
Weber's ideal-type bureaucracy rests on rational-legal authority (hierarchy, rules, impersonality, merit).
New Public Administration (Minnowbrook, 1968) added social equity as a core value.
NPM (Hood 1991; Osborne-Gaebler 1992) = market managerialism, 'steering not rowing'; New Public Service (Denhardt) = 'serving not steering'.
The good-governance paradigm stresses participation, transparency, accountability and responsiveness.
items.source: Wilson (1887); Goodnow (1900); Gulick & Urwick (1937); Weber; Minnowbrook I (1968); Hood (1991); Osborne & Gaebler (1992); Denhardt & Denhardt (2003)

items.title: Administrative Ideas in Kautilya's Arthashastra
items.body:
### Kautilya's Arthashastra and the Saptanga theory

**In one line**
Kautilya's Arthashastra is India's earliest systematic treatise on administration, economy and statecraft, famous for the Saptanga ('seven limbs') theory of the state.

**Why it is asked**
The Saptanga seven elements, key officers, the espionage system and Yogakshema are precise, India-specific facts that APPSC rewards.

**The story**
The **Arthashastra**, written by **Kautilya (also called Chanakya or Vishnugupta)**, mentor of Chandragupta Maurya, is India's earliest systematic work on administration, economy and statecraft (in Sanskrit, 15 books and 180 chapters). Its best-known idea is the **Saptanga** theory, which sees the state as a body with **seven limbs (prakriti)** that must all be healthy. Kautilya also set out a working administration: a **Mantriparishad** (council of ministers whose advice was not binding), merit-chosen higher civil servants (**Amatyas/Mantrins**), a large body of departmental **superintendents (Adhyakshas)**, and an elaborate **espionage** network of spies (**gudhapurushas**) to watch officials and gauge public mood. He insisted the king's cardinal duty was **Yogakshema** — the welfare and security of subjects — and laid down detailed norms on taxation, salaries, audit, punishment (**Danda-niti**) and anti-corruption.

**Picture it — Saptanga, the seven limbs**

| Element (Prakriti) | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Swami | The king (sovereign) |
| Amatya | Ministers and civil servants |
| Janapada | Territory and people |
| Durga | Fort |
| Kosha | Treasury |
| Danda / Bala | Army or force |
| Mitra | Ally |

**Terms explained**
- **Saptanga** — 'seven limbs'; the seven essential elements of a state.
- **Mantriparishad** — the council of ministers advising the king (advice not binding).
- **Adhyakshas** — superintendents heading departments (mines, agriculture, trade, weights).
- **Gudhapurushas** — secret agents or spies in Kautilya's intelligence network.
- **Yogakshema** — the king's duty to ensure subjects' welfare and security.
- **Danda-niti** — the science of punishment and the enforcement of order.

**A memorable line**
Kautilya warned that just as one cannot tell when a fish drinks water, one cannot tell when an official misappropriates revenue — an early note on the ever-present risk of corruption.

**Don't confuse**
- **Swami vs Amatya** — Swami is the king (sovereign); Amatya is the ministers and civil servants.
- **Mantriparishad vs Amatyas** — the council of ministers (advisory body) versus the higher civil service (the officials).

**Remember it**
Saptanga = 'Swami And Janata Deserve Kosha, Danda, Mitra' (S-A-J-D-K-D-M).

**TL;DR**
- Arthashastra by Kautilya (Chanakya/Vishnugupta) = India's earliest treatise on administration and statecraft.
- Saptanga = seven limbs: Swami, Amatya, Janapada, Durga, Kosha, Danda, Mitra.
- Mantriparishad advises; Amatyas/Mantrins are merit-chosen civil servants; Adhyakshas head departments.
- A vast espionage network (gudhapurushas) checked officials; Yogakshema = the king's duty to ensure subjects' welfare.
keyPoints: Arthashastra by Kautilya (Chanakya/Vishnugupta) = India's earliest systematic treatise on administration and statecraft.
Saptanga theory = seven limbs: Swami, Amatya, Janapada, Durga, Kosha, Danda, Mitra.
Mantriparishad = council of ministers; Amatyas/Mantrins = higher civil servants chosen on merit.
Adhyakshas = departmental superintendents; a vast espionage network (gudhapurushas) checked officials.
Yogakshema = the king's duty to ensure subjects' welfare and security; detailed anti-corruption and audit norms.
items.mnemonic: Saptanga: 'Swami And Janata Deserve Kosha, Danda, Mitra' (S-A-J-D-K-D-M).
items.source: Kautilya's Arthashastra (Saptanga theory; administrative organisation; Yogakshema)

items.title: Mughal Administration
items.body:
### The Mughal administrative system

**In one line**
The Mughals, especially Akbar, ran a centralised bureaucratic monarchy with great officers at the centre, the mansabdari rank system for nobles, and a layered provincial structure.

**Why it is asked**
The central officers, the Zat-Sawar meaning in mansabdari, Todar Mal's revenue system and the provincial hierarchy are high-frequency, factual MCQ items.

**The story**
The Mughals (especially **Akbar**) built a **centralised administration** with the emperor at the apex, assisted by great officers of state. The nobility was organised through the **mansabdari system**, in which every officer held a **mansab (rank)** carrying two numbers — **Zat** (personal rank and pay) and **Sawar** (the number of cavalry/horsemen to maintain). Mansabdars were **paid in cash or by jagir** (a revenue assignment); the system was **non-hereditary and transferable**, which kept the nobility in check. Land revenue, the state's chief income, was systematised by Raja **Todar Mal's Zabti/Dahsala system (around 1580)**, which fixed revenue on a **ten-year average** of yields and prices (other systems like Kankut, Batai and Nasaq also existed). The empire was divided into provinces under a layered hierarchy, and Akbar organised it into **15 Subahs** (later about 20).

**Picture it — central officers**

| Office | Charge |
|---|---|
| Wazir / Diwan | Revenue and finance |
| Mir Bakshi | Military pay, mansabdari, intelligence |
| Khan-i-Saman | Royal household and karkhanas |
| Sadr-us-Sudur | Religious affairs, grants and charity |
| Qazi-ul-Quzat | Chief judge (justice) |

**Provincial hierarchy**

| Level | Head | Charge |
|---|---|---|
| Subah (province) | Subedar / Nazim | General administration |
| Sarkar (district) | Faujdar | Law and order |
| Pargana | Shiqdar; Amil/Amalguzar | Administration; revenue |
| Village | Muqaddam, Patwari | Village affairs and records |

**Terms explained**
- **Mansab** — a numerical rank in the Mughal service.
- **Zat vs Sawar** — Zat fixes personal rank and pay; Sawar fixes how many horsemen the holder must maintain.
- **Jagir** — an assignment of land revenue given in place of a cash salary.
- **Dahsala / Zabti** — Todar Mal's system assessing revenue on a ten-year average of yields and prices.
- **Subah / Sarkar / Pargana** — province / district / sub-district in the Mughal structure.

**Don't confuse**
- **Zat vs Sawar** — Zat = personal rank and pay; Sawar = cavalry obligation. Candidates often swap these.
- **Wazir/Diwan vs Mir Bakshi** — the Diwan handled revenue and finance; the Mir Bakshi handled the military and mansabdari.

**Remember it**
'Mansab = Zat (rank/pay) + Sawar (horsemen); Todar Mal = ten-year average revenue.'

**TL;DR**
- Central officers: Wazir/Diwan (revenue), Mir Bakshi (military/mansabdari), Khan-i-Saman (household), Sadr-us-Sudur (religious), Qazi (justice).
- Mansabdari (Akbar): Zat = personal rank/pay, Sawar = cavalry to maintain; non-hereditary, paid in cash or jagir.
- Todar Mal's Zabti/Dahsala (around 1580) assessed revenue on a ten-year average.
- Provincial order: Subah (Subedar) → Sarkar (Faujdar) → Pargana (Shiqdar/Amil) → Village; Akbar had 15 Subahs (later ~20).
keyPoints: Central officers: Wazir/Diwan (revenue), Mir Bakshi (military/mansabdari), Khan-i-Saman (household), Sadr-us-Sudur (religious), Qazi (justice).
Mansabdari (Akbar): Zat = personal rank/pay, Sawar = cavalry to be maintained; non-hereditary, paid in cash or jagir.
Todar Mal's Zabti/Dahsala system (c.1580) assessed revenue on a ten-year average of yields and prices.
Provincial hierarchy: Subah (Subedar) > Sarkar (Faujdar) > Pargana (Shiqdar/Amil) > Village.
Akbar divided the empire into 15 Subahs (later ~20).
items.source: Standard accounts of Mughal administration (Ain-i-Akbari; Mansabdari; Todar Mal's Dahsala)

items.title: Legacy of British Rule — Charter Acts, ICS & Portfolio System
items.body:
### British administrative legacy — Charter Acts, the ICS and the portfolio system

**In one line**
British rule built India's modern civil service through the Charter Acts, created the Indian Civil Service (the 'steel frame'), and introduced the portfolio system that foreshadowed cabinet government.

**Why it is asked**
Which Charter Act did what, the 'father of the civil service', the first Indian in the ICS, and the portfolio system are precise facts tested directly.

**The story**
The civil service evolved through the **Charter Acts**. The **1793** Act saw Cornwallis organise the **covenanted civil service** (recruitment by Company patronage); the **1813** Act renewed the charter and ended the Company's trade monopoly (except tea and the China trade); the **1833** Act created the post of **Governor-General of India** (Bentinck) and saw Macaulay propose open competition (not then implemented); and the **1853** Act finally introduced **open competitive examination**, ending patronage.
**Cornwallis** is called the **'father of the civil service in India'** for professionalising it. The first competitive exam was held in **London in 1855**, and **Satyendranath Tagore** became the **first Indian in the ICS in 1863**. The **Aitchison Committee (1886)** and later reforms Indianised recruitment, and exams began in India (Allahabad, 1922). The ICS was dubbed the **'steel frame' of India** (Lloyd George, 1922). Separately, **Lord Canning** introduced the **portfolio system**, formalised by the **Indian Councils Act, 1861**.

**Picture it — the Charter Acts**

| Act | Administrative significance |
|---|---|
| Charter Act 1793 | Cornwallis organised the covenanted civil service; recruitment by patronage |
| Charter Act 1813 | Renewed charter; Company trade monopoly ended (except tea and China trade) |
| Charter Act 1833 | Created the Governor-General of India; Macaulay proposed open competition (not implemented) |
| Charter Act 1853 | Introduced open competitive examination, ending patronage |

**Terms explained**
- **Covenanted civil service** — the senior Company service whose members signed a covenant (agreement); forerunner of the ICS.
- **Patronage vs open competition** — jobs given by favour versus jobs won by exam on merit.
- **Portfolio system** — distributing government business among individual council members, each handling a department (a forerunner of the cabinet).
- **'Steel frame'** — Lloyd George's 1922 phrase for the ICS as the durable core of the administrative state.

**Enduring legacies**
Rule of law, a permanent civil service, all-India services, the secretariat system, the district Collector, a codified legal system, budgeting and audit (CAG), and local self-government (Ripon, 1882).

**Don't confuse**
- **1833 vs 1853 Charter Act** — 1833 created the Governor-General of India; 1853 introduced open competition for the civil service.
- **Cornwallis vs Canning** — Cornwallis is the father of the civil service; Canning introduced the portfolio system.

**Remember it**
'1853 = open exam; London 1855 = first exam; Satyendranath Tagore 1863 = first Indian; ICS = steel frame.'

**TL;DR**
- Charter Act 1793 (Cornwallis) organised the covenanted service; 1853 introduced open competition.
- Charter Act 1833 created the Governor-General of India.
- Cornwallis = father of the civil service; first ICS exam London 1855; Satyendranath Tagore first Indian (1863); ICS = 'steel frame' (1922).
- Portfolio system introduced by Lord Canning, formalised by the Indian Councils Act 1861.
keyPoints: Charter Act 1793 (Cornwallis) organised the covenanted civil service; 1853 introduced open competition, ending patronage.
Charter Act 1833 created the Governor-General of India; Macaulay's competition proposal was not then implemented.
Cornwallis = 'father of the civil service in India'; first ICS exam London 1855; Satyendranath Tagore first Indian (1863).
ICS was dubbed the 'steel frame' of India (Lloyd George, 1922).
Portfolio system introduced by Lord Canning, formalised by the Indian Councils Act 1861.
British legacies: rule of law, permanent civil service, all-India services, secretariat, district Collector, CAG audit, local self-government.
items.source: Charter Acts 1793-1853; Indian Councils Act 1861; history of the Indian Civil Service

items.title: Civil Services, Reforms & the AP Administrative Structure
items.body:
### Civil services, administrative reforms and the AP structure

**In one line**
Part XIV of the Constitution governs the civil services, the two Administrative Reforms Commissions proposed major reforms, and Andhra Pradesh runs a Secretariat-district-mandal structure with a doorstep village/ward secretariat system.

**Why it is asked**
The exact articles (309-312), the three All India Services, the ARC facts and the AP numbers (districts, village/ward secretariats) are precise, frequently tested points.

**The story**
**Part XIV of the Constitution (Articles 308-323)**, 'Services under the Union and the States', is the constitutional basis of the civil services. **Article 309** covers recruitment and conditions, **Article 310** states the **doctrine of pleasure** (services hold office during the pleasure of the President or Governor), **Article 311** gives **safeguards** against arbitrary dismissal, and **Article 312** lets Parliament create a **new All India Service** only on a **Rajya Sabha resolution passed by two-thirds** of members present and voting. The **three All India Services** are the IAS, IPS and the Indian Forest Service (created 1966), governed by the **All India Services Act, 1951**. The services provide a permanent, neutral, merit-based executive — 'the steel frame' of the state.
Reform came through two commissions, and Andhra Pradesh adds its own administrative structure on top of this national framework.

**Picture it — the two ARCs**

| Commission | Year | Chair | Output |
|---|---|---|---|
| First ARC | 1966 | Morarji Desai (later K. Hanumanthaiya) | 20 reports (1966-70) |
| Second ARC | 2005 | Veerappa Moily (later V. Ramachandran) | 15 reports (2005-09) |

**Terms explained**
- **Doctrine of pleasure** — the rule that government servants hold office at the pleasure of the President or Governor (Article 310), subject to Article 311 safeguards.
- **All India Services** — services common to the Union and states (IAS, IPS, Indian Forest Service).
- **ARC** — Administrative Reforms Commission, set up to recommend reforms to Indian administration.
- **Grama/Ward Sachivalayam** — Andhra Pradesh's village and ward secretariats for doorstep service delivery.

**Second ARC and AP structure**
The 2nd ARC's first report was **'Right to Information — Master Key to Good Governance'**. In Andhra Pradesh, the **State Secretariat (Amaravati)**, headed by the **Chief Secretary**, is the headquarters. For district administration, after the **April 2022** reorganisation AP had **26 districts**, raised to **28** (Polavaram and Markapuram) from **31 December 2025**; each is headed by a **Collector and District Magistrate**, with Revenue Divisions (RDO/Sub-Collector) and **Mandals** (Tahsildar/MRO). The **Grama and Ward Sachivalayam system**, launched **2 October 2019**, set up about **15,004 village** and **3,842 ward** secretariats, supported by Grama/Ward Volunteers, to deliver services at citizens' doorsteps.

**Don't confuse**
- **Article 310 vs 311** — 310 is the doctrine of pleasure; 311 is the safeguard against arbitrary dismissal.
- **First vs Second ARC** — First ARC (1966, Morarji Desai, 20 reports); Second ARC (2005, Veerappa Moily, 15 reports).

**Remember it**
'309 recruit, 310 pleasure, 311 safeguard, 312 new AIS (two-thirds Rajya Sabha).'

**TL;DR**
- Part XIV (Articles 308-323): 309 recruitment, 310 doctrine of pleasure, 311 dismissal safeguards, 312 new AIS via a two-thirds Rajya Sabha resolution.
- Three All India Services = IAS, IPS, Indian Forest Service (1966); All India Services Act 1951.
- First ARC (1966, Morarji Desai) = 20 reports; Second ARC (2005, Veerappa Moily) = 15 reports; its first report was on RTI.
- AP: 28 districts (26 after April 2022, 28 from 31 December 2025); Grama/Ward Sachivalayam launched 2 October 2019 (~15,004 village, 3,842 ward secretariats).
keyPoints: Part XIV (Art 308-323) governs services; Art 309 (recruitment), 310 (doctrine of pleasure), 311 (dismissal safeguards), 312 (new AIS via 2/3 Rajya Sabha resolution).
Three All India Services = IAS, IPS, Indian Forest Service (1966); governed by the All India Services Act 1951.
First ARC (1966, Morarji Desai) gave 20 reports; Second ARC (2005, Veerappa Moily) gave 15 reports.
2nd ARC's first report = 'Right to Information — Master Key to Good Governance'.
AP has 28 districts (26 after the April 2022 reorganisation, 28 from 31 December 2025); Secretariat at Amaravati headed by the Chief Secretary; district headed by Collector-cum-District Magistrate.
AP Grama/Ward Sachivalayam launched 2 October 2019 — ~15,004 village and 3,842 ward secretariats with volunteers for doorstep service delivery.
items.source: Constitution of India Part XIV, Art 308-312; All India Services Act 1951; ARC-I (1966) & 2nd ARC (2005) arc.gov.in; AP reorganisation (2022) & Grama/Ward Sachivalayam Dept (2019)
